concept.body: A cyclic quadrilateral has all four vertices on one circle, and its OPPOSITE angles are supplementary (each pair halves two arcs that tile the full 360°). The converse also holds, making the supplement test a complete membership check. Rectangles, squares, and isosceles trapezoids always pass; other parallelograms and kites generally fail.

widget.prompt: Cyclic quadrilateral, one angle 70°. Its opposite angle = ?

steps.body: A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four vertices on one circle. Its signature: **opposite angles are supplementary.** Why: opposite angles are inscribed angles opening onto complementary arcs — the two arcs together make the whole 360°, so the two angles halve it: 180° between them.

explanationVariants: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180: C = 180 − 95 = 85°.

widget.prompt: Cyclic quadrilateral ABCD has angle A = 95°. Find the opposite angle C.

commonErrors.feedback: 95° copies A — opposite angles SUPPLEMENT in a cyclic quadrilateral: 180 − 95 = 85°.
265 = 360 − 95 charges A against the whole circle — the pair shares only 180: 85°.
47.5 halves — the relationship is a supplement, not a halving: 85°.

steps.body: The proof in one line: angle A halves arc BCD, angle C halves arc DAB, and those arcs tile the whole circle — A + C = ½(360) = 180. The CONVERSE holds too: if a quadrilateral's opposite angles are supplementary, a circle passes through all four vertices. Supplementarity is the entrance ticket.

explanationVariants: Check a supplement: 88 + 92 = 180 ✓ — the converse admits it to a circle.
Opposite pairs 88/92 and 105/75 both hit 180: cyclic.

widget.prompt: A quadrilateral has consecutive angles 88°, 105°, 92°, 75°. Is it cyclic?

options.label: Yes — opposite pairs (88, 92) and (105, 75) each sum to 180°
options.feedback: Both supplements check, so the converse seats all four vertices on one circle.

options.label: No — the angles aren't all equal
options.feedback: Equality isn't required (that's a rectangle's privilege) — SUPPLEMENTARY opposite pairs are, and both pairs pass: cyclic.

options.label: No — 88 + 105 ≠ 180
options.feedback: 88 and 105 are CONSECUTIVE — the test pairs OPPOSITE angles: 88 + 92 = 180 and 105 + 75 = 180. Cyclic.

options.label: Cannot tell from angles alone
options.feedback: For this question angles suffice — the supplement test is a full characterization (both directions).

explanationVariants: A quadrilateral is cyclic iff opposite angles supplement. Rectangles: 90 + 90 = 180 always. General parallelograms: opposite angles are EQUAL, so they'd each need to be 90.
Rectangles (and squares) pass automatically; isosceles trapezoids do too; other parallelograms fail.

widget.prompt: From the quadrilateral course's cast, which is ALWAYS cyclic?

options.label: The rectangle — every angle 90°, so opposite pairs always hit 180°
options.feedback: Rectangles (squares included) pass the supplement test automatically — their circumscribed circle's center is the diagonals' crossing, with the congruent diagonals as diameters.

options.label: Every parallelogram
options.feedback: Parallelograms make opposite angles EQUAL — equal AND supplementary forces 90°, so only the rectangles among them are cyclic.

options.label: Every kite
options.feedback: A kite is cyclic only when its two side-angles are right — generic kites fail the supplement test.

options.label: The general trapezoid
options.feedback: Only the ISOSCELES trapezoid is always cyclic (its base-angle pairs supplement across the parallel sides) — generic trapezoids fail.

steps.body: Two opposite corners, one circle, one constraint.

widget.prompt: Make the OPPOSITE angle read 110°. Watch the two angles as you drag: they are locked together.
widget.successFeedback: An arc of 140° puts 70° at P, and the opposite corner takes the rest of the circle: 180 − 70 = 110°. The two arcs make a full 360°, so the two angles must make 180° — always, whatever shape the quadrilateral takes.
widget.lowFeedback: The opposite angle is still under 110°. It is 180° minus the angle at P, so shrinking the arc raises it.
widget.highFeedback: The opposite angle has gone past 110°. Opening the arc raises the angle at P, which lowers its opposite.

predict.prompt: You'll drag the arc bigger, growing one angle of the cyclic quadrilateral. Its OPPOSITE angle will…
predict.reveal: Opposite angles watch complementary arcs — one sees an arc, the other sees the REST of the circle, and those two arcs always total 360°. Halve each and the angles are locked at 180° together: one grows, the other must give way.

cml.actionGoal: Move points on a circle while arc, central-angle, and inscribed-angle measures update together.

widget.prompt: A cyclic quadrilateral has one angle of 117°. Its opposite angle = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 243 = 360 − 117 uses the full circle — the opposite pair shares 180°: 63°.

hints: Opposite angles A and C supplement: 2x + 3x = 180.

widget.prompt: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, angle A = 2x and its opposite angle C = 3x. Find angle C in degrees.

commonErrors.feedback: 72° = 2x is angle A — the question asks C = 3x = 108°.
90° assumes a rectangle — the supplement equation 5x = 180 gives x = 36, C = 108°.

takeaways: Cyclic quadrilateral: opposite angles supplementary — they halve complementary arcs of the full 360°.
The converse holds: supplementary opposite pairs guarantee a circumscribing circle.
Always cyclic from the quadrilateral cast: rectangles, squares, isosceles trapezoids; parallelograms only when they're rectangles.
steps.teaser: That closes the circle course — angles, chords, tangents, powers, and the arcs that price them all.
